format: Result-first self-test: 'I tried X for N nights, the outcome stated in line one'

hook.visual: Phone screen filmed at arm's length showing sleep-tracker graph, finger pointing at a flat stretch where the old 3am gap used to be
hook.audio: Night four was still rubbish. Night nine is the reason I'm filming this.

script: Night four was still rubbish. Night nine is the reason I'm filming this.
I've woken up at 3am, basically every night, for about two years.
Not stressed. Not needing the loo. Just awake, staring at the ceiling.
So I tried one capsule of magnesium glycinate, 30 minutes before bed. That's it.
Nothing happened for the first five nights and I nearly gave up.
Then one morning I realised I hadn't seen 3am on my phone in a while.
It's 300mg, there's no melatonin in it, and I don't wake up foggy.
It's not magic. It took a week and a half to notice anything.
But I haven't checked the time in the middle of the night since night nine.
caption: What time do you wake up at? Mine was always 3am.
share_reason: Someone who wakes up at 3am sends this to their partner who watches them do it, or to the group chat where everyone complains about being tired
comment_trigger: The stated 3am time makes people name their own wake-up time; the 'nothing happened for five nights' admission invites 'how long did it actually take you'
why_views: Opening with a dated before/after on a real tracker screen shows the result before any context, and the admission that nights 1-5 failed buys credibility from a sceptical audience in the first second.

format: POV text overlay, silent, trending audio, shot in real conditions

hook.visual: Dark bedroom, face lit only by phone screen, eyes open, ceiling above

script: silent throughout — text overlays carry the whole story over slow handheld shots in the dark
on_screen_text: not stressed. not thirsty. just awake.
falling asleep was never my problem
so I stopped buying sleep sprays and gummies
and tried 300mg magnesium glycinate. one capsule.
caption: 3am club, what's your exact time?
share_reason: Sent silently at 2am from one insomniac to another as an 'this is literally me' tag — no audio needed, works on mute in bed
comment_trigger: 'What's your exact time' makes hundreds of people post 3:04, 3:12, 4am — cheap, high-volume comments and an argument about why it's always 3am
why_views: Filmed in the exact situation the viewer is in while scrolling — dark room, phone light, 3:07am on screen — so the hook is recognition rather than information, which holds mute viewers.

format: Ranking with the controversial pick last: '4 things I tried, ranked worst to best'

hook.visual: Four items lined up on a duvet: a lavender spray, a weighted eye mask, a sleep tea box, a plain white capsule bottle. Hand sweeps the spray straight off the bed.
hook.audio: Four things I bought to fix waking up at 3am, ranked, and number one is going to annoy people.

script: Four things I bought to fix waking up at 3am, ranked, and number one is going to annoy people.
Four: the pillow spray. Smells lovely. Did absolutely nothing at 3am.
Three: the sleep tea. Made me get up at 3am to wee instead. Worse.
Two: the weighted eye mask. Genuinely nice. Helped me fall asleep, not stay asleep.
One: the boring one. 300mg magnesium glycinate, one capsule, 30 minutes before bed.
No melatonin, so no hangover feeling in the morning, which was my whole issue with the other stuff.
Took me about a week and a half before I noticed anything, so don't judge it on night two.
The reviews are all the same sentence: 'I stopped waking up at 3am.' That was it for me too.
Annoying, because I wanted the answer to be the eye mask. It was the £24 bottle of boring.
So: four things, and the one I'd buy again is the one with no smell, no ritual, no vibe.
caption: Defend the pillow spray in the comments, I dare you.
share_reason: Sent to the friend who owns all four of these things and swears by the spray, as a wind-up
comment_trigger: Openly ranking beloved products last — pillow spray and sleep tea fans will argue, and people will add their own #1
why_views: A four-item ranking creates four micro-payoffs plus a pre-announced controversial ending, so the viewer stays for the reveal instead of dropping at the product mention.

format: Anti-sell: 'reasons you should not buy this' — objections stated before the pitch

hook.visual: Creator holding the bottle, then setting it down and pushing it away from the camera
hook.audio: Three reasons you shouldn't buy this, from someone who takes it every night.

script: Three reasons you shouldn't buy this, from someone who takes it every night.
One: it's slow. It took me about nine nights. If you want tonight to be different, this isn't it.
Two: it's £24 a month on subscription. That's a real cost for something this undramatic.
Three: it doesn't knock you out. There's no melatonin in it. You won't feel drugged.
If falling asleep is your problem, I'm honestly not sure this is your thing.
Mine was staying asleep. Awake at 3am, every night, for about two years.
One capsule, 300mg magnesium glycinate, half an hour before bed, nothing else changed.
Two thousand-odd reviews and they all say the same boring sentence about 3am. So does mine now.
So don't buy it for tonight. Buy it if you're willing to be unimpressed for a week.
caption: Would you give something 10 nights before deciding?
share_reason: Sceptics send it to other sceptics — it's the rare supplement video that leads with the downsides, so it reads as safe to forward
comment_trigger: Stating the price out loud splits the comments into 'that's expensive' vs 'cheaper than my sleep', and 'this isn't for you if...' makes people declare which problem they have
why_views: Opening by pushing the product away inverts the expected ad structure, so the sceptical viewer stays to hear the criticism they were already forming.

format: Reading real reviews out loud and reacting to the one repeated phrase

hook.visual: Phone held close to camera, thumb scrolling a wall of reviews fast; scroll stops hard on a highlighted line
hook.audio: I scrolled two thousand reviews and the same seven words keep coming up.

script: I scrolled two thousand reviews and the same seven words keep coming up.
'I stopped waking up at 3am.' That one. Again. And again.
Not 'life changing'. Not 'best sleep ever'. Just that.
Which is weirdly the only kind of review I trust, because it's so specific.
So I checked what's actually in it: 300mg magnesium glycinate. No melatonin.
One capsule, 30 minutes before bed. That's the entire instruction.
4.7 stars across 2,100 of them, which for a supplement that does one boring thing is quite a lot.
The reviews also warn you it takes about five to ten days, which I appreciated.
I'm on night eleven. And I've now got the same seven words as everyone else.
caption: Do you trust a specific review more than a glowing one?
share_reason: Sent to the friend who always says 'reviews are fake' — the point of the video is how to read reviews, not the product
comment_trigger: The claim that vague five-star reviews are less trustworthy than specific ones is a hot take people love to back up or dispute with their own examples
why_views: A fast review scroll that slams to a stop on one highlighted sentence is pure visual curiosity, and the repeated phrase gives the video a built-in payoff to wait for.

format: Mid-process diary entry: 'day N of something, filmed at the moment of doubt'

hook.visual: Creator in the kitchen at night, unwashed hair, holding a capsule between finger and thumb up to the camera light
hook.audio: Day six of this and I'm about to say something I'll probably regret.

script: Day six of this and I'm about to say something I'll probably regret.
I think it's not working. Six nights, one capsule each night, 30 minutes before bed.
Still woke up at 3am on nights two, four and five.
The company literally tells you it takes five to ten days, so I know I'm being impatient.
It's 300mg magnesium glycinate. No melatonin, so there's nothing to make me feel it working.
Which is the annoying part. There's no effect to report. Just data I don't have yet.
I'm going to keep going to night fourteen and come back either way.
If it doesn't work I'll say so and I'll say what I paid.
Update at day fourteen. Save this if you want to know whether I regret it.
caption: Day 14 update coming. Guess now: works or doesn't?
share_reason: Sent to a friend who's mid-argument about whether supplements do anything, as a live experiment to follow
comment_trigger: Asking people to predict the outcome, plus openly doubting the product, pulls in both 'give it time, mine took 10 days' and 'it's a placebo' replies arguing with each other
why_views: Admitting failure at day six is the opposite of what viewers expect from a product video, and the promised day-14 update turns the open loop into follows, saves and return views.
